extracted.intended_audience: reporters, editors, multimedia journalists, and freelancers who cover crime and crime victims
extracted.subtask_description: Practical ethical and professional guidelines for journalists producing news stories (Act I–III) about crime and crime victims, including interviewing, multimedia coverage, working with service providers, and privacy/legal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect individuality of victims' trauma responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims can show a wide range of emotions — anger, fear, denial, remorse, frustration, sadness — or may appear emotionless (e.g., PTSD). Reporters should not mistake lack of affect for lack of caring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect victims for the individuality of their responses to trauma; understand that atypical reactions can be symptoms of trauma or disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish rapport before asking hard questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Give victims a chance to relax and feel secure before asking them to recount traumatic experiences and comment on what happened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize potential damage from tough questions by building trust first; do not push too fast or too hard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and understand survivor guilt
rubrics_metrics.description: Survivors may feel guilty for living while others died; these feelings can intensify over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express reassurance but do not expect to "cure" the victim; be aware survivor guilt may persist and affect interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer verbal consolation but do not touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledging a victim’s suffering is appropriate, but physical contact (hugs, squeezes) is unwise and can intrude on a victim’s boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show compassion via words, body language, and facial reactions (nod, concerned smile). Avoid touching; even asking permission to touch can put victims in an awkward position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the burdens of 'continuing mystery' cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims (e.g., parents of missing children) often experience a roller coaster of hope and despair and heightened fear if perpetrators are uncaught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and understand the victim’s particular circumstances to help put them at ease; apply anniversary-story sensitivity principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal-profile reporting: avoid forcing victims into a mold
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature stories about recovering victims should not push the subject into a preconceived formula; victims have good days and bad days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interview the victim more than once to ensure apparent courage or depression is accurately portrayed; avoid simple, single-encounter judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'journalist as betrayer' dynamic
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing quick rapport can lead victims to view the reporter as a friend; victims may feel betrayed if the published profile differs from expectations or if their contribution is cut or a story cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about editorial decisions where possible; manage expectations, explain cancellations sensitively, and be mindful that editorial selection (dramatic/photogenic reasons) can hurt victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure freelancer accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations increasingly rely on freelancers; those freelancers must employ best practices when dealing with victims and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should work with freelancers to ensure they understand and follow victim-sensitive practices and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experts appropriately and respectfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes from professionals (physicians, psychologists, sociologists) can be useful but may feel insulting to victims if they analyze personalities, motives, or weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and respect victims’ perspectives as experts on their own victimization; be cautious about using expert commentary that could be perceived as demeaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify reliable experts and advocate sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Victim advocates and service providers can supply statistics/trends, 'myths and facts', relevant laws, overviews of victimization dynamics, research-based information, community resources, and referrals to reliable local/state/national experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sources for accurate, context-rich reporting; treat victim advocates as both advocates and informational resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'poster child' problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a single victim to represent an entire category of victims; each victim’s experience is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist symbolic or representative casting that erases individuality or implies universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect multimedia coverage and prepare victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Online reporting increasingly mixes text, audio, video, and images; reporters (including mobile journalists or 'mojos') may gather multiple media types in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the likelihood that victims will appear in multimedia formats; prepare and inform victims about what multimedia exposure means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train print reporters who shoot video on victim issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Print reporters asked to shoot video may not understand how intrusive moving images can be and the additional burden on victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide training on videotaping victims with sensitivity and dignity; training needn't produce broadcast-quality video but should cover ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider global reach and permanence of online content
rubrics_metrics.description: Online articles are globally accessible and can remain retrievable via search engines for years, potentially exposing victims long after they wish to move on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include victims and victim organizations in discussions about archiving and corrections policies; be mindful of long-term reputational and privacy impacts when publishing names or sensitive details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inform citizen journalists about victim issues
rubrics_metrics.description: User-generated content (iReport, citizen video/photos) can be valuable but citizen journalists are often untrained in victim-sensitive reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should post guidance (like this guide) to help citizen journalists understand victim needs and ethical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect victims from abusive anonymous online comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Unmoderated anonymous comments often include abusive or insensitive postings that can harm victims and those who care for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should work with victims to develop moderation policies; until filtering is reliable, take whatever steps are necessary (manual moderation, pre-screening) to prevent abusive postings on stories involving crime victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support and prioritize Act III high-impact stories
rubrics_metrics.description: In-depth Act III pieces can deepen public understanding of crime, victimization, and policy and give victims a voice, but they require significant time and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News organizations should be encouraged and supported to devote resources to major projects and series that provide social, political, economic, or cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand types and roles of victim service providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Three broad categories: victim advocates (often lobbying/advocacy), victim service providers (paid positions in agencies with organizational loyalties), and citizen volunteers (comfort and practical aid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize differences: advocates may pursue publicity, service providers may prefer victims refrain from media before/during trial, and volunteers may or may not have media training. Use groups as sources and buffers appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactively build relationships with advocates and service providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop rapport and two-way understanding between news organizations and those who work with victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite advocates and providers to advisory panels and editorial board presentations; offer newsroom tours; increase transparency and feedback opportunities to help them understand journalism and to allow them to comment on coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt ethics policies emphasizing minimizing harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow guiding principles (Poynter/ Society for Professional Journalists): (1) seek truth and report it fully, (2) act independently, (3) minimize harm, (4) be accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize minimizing harm does not mean eliminating it; weigh public benefit (utility) against potential harm and place burden on journalists to avoid causing undue pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance victim privacy with public's right to know
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional and statutory law (FOIA, state sunshine laws, court decisions) define access but also create tensions with victims' privacy interests; law and practice vary across jurisdictions and agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate access with law enforcement, consider evolving privacy norms (post-9/11/Internet effects), and be aware that the pendulum has tended toward greater privacy protection in recent years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intrusion and harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can be found to intrude on solitude (trespass, hidden surveillance, fraudulent entry). Reporters may stand on public sidewalks but repeated doorbell ringing/telephone calls can be harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay on public property, avoid trespass or use of eavesdropping/hidden devices, respect state laws on recording telephone calls, and identify oneself as a reporter; be mindful of Gallela v. Onassis precedent about stalking/harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle photography and filming with privacy sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: People have an expectation of privacy in their homes; use of telephoto lenses to film into private spaces or recording in places with an expectation of privacy is impermissible in many states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscure faces/identifiers in stock photos or file footage that portray people in unflattering ways; obtain consent when necessary and avoid invasive visual practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow courtroom camera rules and consider victim safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Most states permit cameras in courtroom subject to operating rules; federal courts generally disallow cameras. Victims may have privacy/safety concerns even where cameras are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult state court operating rules (when applicable), coordinate with court personnel, and consider accommodations or petitions from prosecutors/advocates to protect victims (e.g., witness protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat 'private facts' and public records carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Information in the public record is generally open to the press (Cox Broadcasting v. Cohn; Florida Star v. B.J.F.), but courts and legislatures have sometimes protected particularly sensitive materials (e.g., autopsy photos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify whether material is public record and weigh newsworthiness against harm; be aware of state statutes that may restrict publication of certain facts or images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid publishing false or reckless information (false light and accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be held liable for false light or similar claims, courts look at whether the news organization knew information was false and recklessly published it. Malicious intent standards may apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise responsibility to determine facts before publication; correct errors promptly; avoid publishing unverified assertions that could portray victims inaccurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify as a reporter when approaching victims (with narrow exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethically and legally, reporters should identify themselves when approaching crime victims; undercover or deceptive approaches are increasingly constrained and usually permissible only in limited investigative contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer transparency in approaches to victims; when deception is contemplated for investigative work, weigh legal/ethical limits and increasing judicial scrutiny.
